statement: A balance has two pans. You have three weights: 1 g, 3 g and 8 g. The object goes on one pan, and each weight can go on either pan or be left off. How many different whole-number masses, in grams, can be weighed exactly in a single weighing?

choices.misconception: I only put weights on the pan opposite the object, which gives just the 7 different totals of the weights.
I allowed one weight against one other weight but never two weights against one, so I missed 6 and 10.
I counted the 27 ways to place the weights, removed the empty one and halved for mirror images, without checking that every result is different.
I counted every way of placing each weight left, right or off, apart from all off, without noticing that many give a repeated or negative mass.

hints: A weight on the same pan as the object counts as a minus.

Each mass you can weigh is a total of the form plus or minus 1, plus or minus 3, plus or minus 8, with some weights left out. List the positive totals systematically, starting with the masses up to 12.
The heaviest mass is 1 + 3 + 8 = 12. Check each of 1 to 12: for example 2 = 3 - 1, 5 = 8 - 3, 6 = 8 + 1 - 3 and 10 = 8 + 3 - 1.

solutions.reliable: Putting a weight beside the object subtracts it, so the masses you can weigh are the positive values of a x 1 + b x 3 + c x 8 where each of a, b, c is 1, 0 or -1. The largest is 12. Going through 1 to 12: 1, 2 = 3 - 1, 3, 4 = 3 + 1, 5 = 8 - 3, 6 = 8 + 1 - 3, 7 = 8 - 1, 8, 9 = 8 + 1, 10 = 8 + 3 - 1, 11 = 8 + 3 and 12 = 8 + 3 + 1. Every whole number from 1 to 12 works and nothing larger does, so 12 masses. The transferable idea: in balance puzzles a weight on the object's pan subtracts, which turns sums into signed sums.
solutions.elegant: The weights 1 and 3 alone give every mass from -4 to 4. Adding 8 on the other side then covers 4 to 12, and 1 to 4 are already covered, so every mass from 1 to 12 is possible.

whyOnTest: Balance puzzles test seeing that weights on both pans subtract as well as add, which roughly doubles what a small set can measure.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
